Tech Report: Stephen King's 8 Greatest Book Masterpieces, Ranked

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is simply no one as prolific in the modern literary realm as Stephen King.
  • According to recent reports, with more than five dozen novels and hundreds of short stories, King’s track record of authoring masterpieces is quite high.
  • First published under the pseudonym Richard Bachman, the dystopian thriller The Running Man became an almost prophetic wonder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is simply no one as prolific in the modern literary realm as Stephen King. Dubbed the King of Horror, the genuine genius proved that horror was his wheelhouse, but he could also put out monumental hits in the suspense, crime, science fiction, fantasy, and mystery realms. Between creating iconic characters and crafting tales that have infiltrated our nightmares and then having them cemented into media history through the power of film and television adaptation, King’s influence on entertainment and pop culture is undeniable.

According to recent reports, with more than five dozen novels and hundreds of short stories, King’s track record of authoring masterpieces is quite high. But which of those masterpieces are the very best? We’re here to create eight titles that fit the brief. While fans may have their own list of favorites, this group spans a strong range of themes, genres, and eras. We will mention their impact and adaptations when necessary, but most of our discussion will center around the book itself. What’s your favorite Stephen King book of all time?

First published under the pseudonym Richard Bachman, the dystopian thriller The Running Man became an almost prophetic wonder. Set in a dystopian, economically ruined America in the year 2025, the narrative follows an unemployed, desperate father named Ben Richards who enters a deadly reality TV game show to pay for his gravely ill daughter's medicine. To win a one-billion-dollar prize, Richards must survive for 30 days while being hunted across the country by ruthless professional killers and a bloodthirsty public. As he evades capture across multiple states, he uncovers dark truths about the totalitarian network running the games, culminating in a violent final confrontation. The novel stands out for its relentless pacing, sharp satire of media and inequality, and raw, desperate protagonist.

Sources indicate that A profound novel within King’s catalog, The Running Man anticipated reality television, audience participation, and the public's willingness to treat human suffering as entertainment. Viewers don't just watch the lethal manhunt; they are financially rewarded for turning contestants in, making the audience complicit. Unlike a traditional invincible action hero, Ben Richards is an impoverished, angry, and physically frail man whose rage and desperation to pay for his sick daughter's medical care drive the story with urgent emotional weight. Written in roughly a week, it carries that same urgency in its pacing, moving at a furious clip. The book takes a much darker, grimmer turn, while its two films lean into a campier approach. In 1987, Paul Michael Glaser directed a loose adaptation starring Arnold Schwarzenegger. Then, Edgar Wright took on a more book-accurate version in 2025, the year the book was set, with Glen Powell playing Richards.

What if you had the ability to change history, would you take the opportunity even if it means it will alter the future? That's the main premise of King's daring sci-fi thriller 11/22/63. The novel follows Jake Epping, a high school English teacher who discovers a time portal in the back of a local diner that leads back to the year 1958. Recruited by his dying friend, Jake embarks on a mission to live in the past and prevent the assassination of President John F. Kennedy. Along the way, his prepares get complicated as he falls in love with a small-town librarian, realizes history resists change, and confronts the unforeseen consequences of altering the timeline. A masterful time-travel thriller, 11/22/63 was a daring risk that paid off.

In a recent development, the novel blends a high-stakes story with an intimate, emotionally grounded love story and vivid historical detail. Rather than treating time travel as a simple fix, King presents the past as resistant, pushing back with obstacles and unintended consequences as Jake tries to alter his newfound present. King backed up his nostalgia with extensive research into the era, capturing everyday textures alongside the tension leading up to November 22, 1963. The novel tackles alternate history in an accessible manner where the true horror is fate itself. While the novel features recurring interest in fragile reality and subtle ties to its broader universe, 11/22/63 stands out for its brazen mechanics and heartbreaking romance. The conclusion leaves a lasting impression by weighing personal sacrifice against the broader consequences of changing history. The novel translated perfectly into a self-contained sci-fi miniseries led by James Franco.

If there's one novel that truly defines everything that King is, it's 'Salem's Lot. His second published novel, the horror story follows writer Ben Mears as he returns to his childhood home of Jerusalem's Lot, Maine, to research a local house for a book. He soon discovers that an ancient vampire named Kurt Barlow has moved into the mansion and is turning townspeople into vampires. A small group of residents band together to fight the spreading infection and survive. A genuine horror masterpiece, 'Salem's Lot transplants classic gothic vampire tropes into a richly detailed, modern small-town American setting using the structure of Bram Stoker's Dracula.

Recent findings suggest that 'Salem's Lot is a slow-burning epidemic horror. Suspense builds gradually as isolated disappearances turn into an overwhelming vampiric infection that erodes community trust and normal life. Barlow and his spawn are depicted as genuinely monstrous predators, heightening the dread when ordinary defenses fail. Rather than treating the townspeople as disposable victims, King builds an ensemble of everyday individuals whose secrets, lives, and vulnerabilities make the collapse feel intimate and real. With unshowy prose and a broad portrait of a declining Maine hamlet, the story has been transported to the small screen twice as a miniseries, first with David Soul in 1979 and Rob Lowe in 2004, then as a feature film, the strongest of the three, in 2024 starring Lewis Pullman.

It has been revealed that not only is It a masterpiece, but it also remains a bona fide fan favorite story. The 17th novel written under his own name, it is set in Derry, Maine, where an ancient, shape-shifting entity that preys on children's fears awakens roughly every 27 years to feed, most famously disguised as Pennywise the Dancing Clown. In 1958, a group of seven outcast kids known as the Losers' Club wounds the creature in the town's sewers and swears a blood oath to return if it ever comes back. When the murders resume in 1985, the now-adult friends must confront their repressed childhood trauma and reunite in Derry to destroy the monster permanently. It pairs a sprawling coming-of-age story with layered psychology and cosmic horror for a truly timeless wonder that has remained a part of the entertainment zeitgeist since its release.

Industry observers note that across a massive page count, King does a phenomenal job developing seven distinct outsiders whose friendships and mutual support through shared trauma anchor the narrative against overwhelming fear. It may be King's greatest example of establishing deep character bonds. The story weaves between two dual timelines. By doing so, it highlights how adult memory, repressed trauma, and lost childhood wonder shape a fight against evil. Though Derry functions like a living character with a dark history and cyclical violence, the greatest non-human character is the creature. Pennywise is the iconic face and physical embodiment of the villain; its ability to shift shapes to match each victim's greatest personal fears makes it one of the most terrifying horror villains in history. The horror goes beyond the single monster, as it manifests as abuse, neglect, hate, and adult indifference. It became a runaway bestseller and spawned major adaptations that have kept the story alive, including the original 1990 TV miniseries starring Tim Curry as Pennywise, a two-part film adaptation with Bill Skarsgard as Pennywise, and a brilliant prequel series, It: Welcome to Derry.

In a recent development, four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

It has been revealed that your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Recent findings suggest that king's greatest psychological horror is a writer's ultimate nightmare: Misery. The twisted masterpiece follows bestselling romance author Paul Sheldon, who is rescued from a severe winter car crash in rural Colorado by former nurse Annie Wilkes. Although she claims to be his "number one fan," Annie keeps the injured writer prisoner in her isolated home and uses painkillers to control him. After discovering that Paul has killed off her favorite heroine in his latest book, Annie violently forces him to write a upcoming novel that brings the character back to life. Misery pairs claustrophobic, grounded psychological horror with a sharp allegory about authorship, creative control, and addiction. Unlike many of King's other pieces, there are no supernatural crutches. The true terror comes entirely from human cruelty, mental instability, and physical helplessness.

Industry observers note that misery is an exemplary two-hander. Much of the action traps the injured novelist in a single room in a remote house. Keeping the focus tightly on Paul's survival makes every minute decision and moment of tension feel immediate and personal. That remarked, Annie may be the greatest antagonist King has ever concocted. She swings wildly between folksy warmth, childish logic, and sudden, brutal bouts of intense violence. King uses the novel to explore a writer's nightmare through creative captivity. It captures the grueling mechanics and pressures of writing in a literally literal way. Further, King uses the dynamic between Paul's painkiller dependency, his obsession with writers, and Annie's erratic control as an allegory for addiction during the height of his own struggles with substance abuse. In the end, writing becomes a tool for endurance and escape, shifting the story toward imagination and survival. Misery was brought to the significant screen in 1990 with James Caan as Paul and Kathy Bates, who won an Academy Award for the part, as Annie. It's also been adapted for the stage, and Lizzy Caplan played a younger version of Annie in Castle Rock's second season.

According to recent reports, part of a larger collection of stories, the realist novella Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption remains one of King's finest works. The novella follows Andy Dufresne, an inmate wrongly convicted of murdering his wife and her lover, as he endures decades of life at Shawshank State Prison. Told by fellow prisoner Red, the story tracks Andy's quiet resilience, his financial dealings with corrupt prison staff, and his decades-long initiative to tunnel out of his cell. Through Andy's enduring hope, Red gradually shifts from a cynical convict to someone who believes in redemption. The story blends a gripping prison-escape narrative with a deeply emotional, resonant heart.

Industry observers note that king delivers a grounded crime and prison drama modeled after classic Hollywood storytelling, proving his depth and range as a dramatic writer regardless of genre. He miraculously contrasts grim institutional corruption and despair with quiet perseverance and dignity. The novel reads like a reflective, memory-driven account that makes the narrative feel personal, immediate, and rooted in reality. The bond between Red and Andy is a message of enduring friendship, giving the story emotional weight that lasts well beyond the final page. While key changes occurred between the page and the screen, The Shawshank Redemption, starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman, is hailed as one of the greatest adaptations of King's work.

Few King novels hit as hard as The Stand. The epic post-apocalyptic dark fantasy centers around a devastating global pandemic caused by a weaponized influenza strain known as "Captain Trips." After the virus accidentally escapes a military facility and wipes out over 99% of humanity, the few immune survivors are drawn by a shared dream into an elemental battle between good and evil. The survivors split into two opposing factions, one building a peaceful community around the benevolent 108-year-old Mother Abagail in Boulder, Colorado, and the other gathering under the demonic Randall Flagg in Las Vegas. It all comes to a head in a final confrontation that decides humankind's fate. The epic masterpiece combines a universal battle between good and evil with a grounded, psychological portrait of ordinary people surviving a deadly pandemic.

With an epic scope inspired by The Lord of the Rings, The Stand merges a post-war survival mindset, dark fantasy, and theological themes that divide a broken society. King crafts his story around rich, relatable characters where there is no singular hero but a series of flawed, ordinary individuals whose inner monologues and moral choices drive the narrative. A landmark in King's broader fictional universe, The Stand's original edition was trimmed before an uncut edition arrived in 1990 that truly captured the brilliance of King's storytelling. The Stand has been adapted twice as a miniseries, first in 1994 starring Gary Sinise, Jamey Sheridan, and Molly Ringwald, and then in 2020 featuring Alexander Skarsgård, Whoopi Goldberg, James Marsden, and Odessa Young. The former remains one of the greatest network miniseries ever made.

According to recent reports, here's The Shining! King's third novel is his very best. The Shining is literary horror at its finest. Jack Torrance, a struggling writer and recovering alcoholic, takes a job as the winter caretaker of the isolated Overlook Hotel in Colorado. He brings along his wife, Wendy, and their young son, Danny, who possesses extrasensory psychic abilities known as "the shining" that let him see the hotel's ghastly past and future. Once winter storms cut them off from the outside world, the malevolent supernatural forces inside the hotel prey on Jack's personal demons and push him toward madness, putting his family in grave danger. The Shining pairs supernatural horror with deeply personal psychological drama, turning an isolated gig into a study of addiction, trauma, and family breakdown.

The Shining pulls from King's own personal struggles. The novel's stakes rise as King draws on his experience with alcoholism and frustrations with fatherhood to ground the supernatural story in real, authentic pain. Jack is a man fighting to change, making his unraveling tragic rather than inevitable. Wendy and Danny are given immense depth, showing how past abuse and fear shape the action in the present. The Overlook Hotel is presented as a living force with sentient malice. It functions as a predatory entity that senses weaknesses, feeds on guilt, and exploits individual flaws. With gothic traditions and claustrophobic isolation, King's visceral writing is kept tightly focused on three individuals in one unsettling setting, with sustaining dread established on page one. King has famously disliked the Stanley Kubrick adaptation, as the novel's emotional nuance and character arcs are not nearly the same. And yet, the Jack Nicholson and Shelley Duvall film remains a beacon of prime horror. Though King wrote the 1997 miniseries version starring Steven Weber and Rebecca De Mornay, it pales in comparison.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The great benefit of having clout in Hollywood — aside from fame, fortune, and a standing reservation at any restaurant in town — is being able to say “no.” You don’t have to take any job that pays.
  • Far be it from me to know what exactly went wrong with Schur and Poehler’s new series, but something did, unfortunately, go wrong.
  • Industry observers note that nothing, that is, but the stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The great benefit of having clout in Hollywood — aside from fame, fortune, and a standing reservation at any restaurant in town — is being able to say “no.” You don’t have to take any job that pays. You don’t even have to work year-round. And you certainly don’t have to chase silly trends, like, say — I don’t know — making a comedy that’s also a mystery that’s also a drama? Beloved, funny folks like Amy Poehler and Mike Schur, who earned a huge chunk of their influence through the indelible sitcom, “Parks and Recreation,” should be able to make anything they want! Any way they want! They earned it!

Far be it from me to know what exactly went wrong with Schur and Poehler’s new series, but something did, unfortunately, go wrong. Each 32-35 minute episode strains to wrap up plots that limp to the finish line. Narrative momentum only exists from the minor twists revealed in the final seconds — then the credits roll, the “up next” button lights up, and your natural curiosity over what happens next wins out over your desire to scroll for something better. Worst of all, everything is “light”: The tone is light, the jokes are light, the mystery is light, the drama is light, even the lighting is light. (It’s so bright, all the time, even at night!) Watching “Dig” is like bearing witness to dwindling interest: Whatever originally compelled the “Dig” team to adapt Kate Myers’ 2023 novel, “Excavations” gets spread so thin across the disparate parts of this broad adaptation that there’s almost nothing left.

Industry observers note that nothing, that is, but the stars. Poehler leads an affable cast (astutely assembled by casting directors Allison Jones and Emily Buntyn) as lead archaeologist Elise, a devoted digger (no, not that kind) whose decades in the dirt have earned her respect and admiration but also turned her cynical and closed-off. She’s an accomplished expert in the field who’s been waiting to run her own site for years, working diligently under the tutelage of beloved British professor Neville Wycombe (Hugh Laurie), but events have conspired to keep her from the top job.

Sources indicate that the most obvious concern is also the simplest: Neville has repeatedly promised to retire, only to rescind that promise when it comes time to make it official. This year he swears he’ll step down for real, but Elise knows better than to buy-in, especially when her informal audition (giving the welcome speech to a group of undergrads they call Ugs) exposes her greatest weakness: She’s not an inspiring leader. “I know your default setting is ‘tough love,'” Neville tells Elise, “but please learn to give people some grace.”.

According to recent reports, that advice is put to the test when Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), Elise’s flaky former protégé, shows up at the dig site after abandoning her post five years prior without so much as a goodbye. Returning with a questionable back tattoo that reads “a traveler on the adventure of life” and without any luggage, directions, or direction (as in, for her life), Dylan is a messy 29-year-old trying to sort things out as she turns 30. Luckily, she meets the too-put-together-for-her-own-good Clare (Antonia Thomas), a 39-year-old head preservationist who’s secure in her calling, engaged to Dylan’s ex-boyfriend Gary (Jon Pointing), and always dressed to the nines. (Surprise, surprise: Clare comes from money.).

The two will learn from each other, just as they’ll each learn from Elise, but they should all take more cues from Patty Borkman (Fina Strazza), the 19-year-old intern who’s assigned to be Neville’s assistant. That’s, in part, because Patty is the youngest and eagerist of a central foursome neatly divided by decades (did I mention Elise is 49?), but more so because Patty — as you may have guessed by her last name — is a fizzy vat of quirky energy that Strazza impressively dissipates into a charming, fresh, coming-of-age character.

In a recent development, patty’s voice sounds like a shy version of Cristin Milioti’s adult baby from “30 Rock.” She wears silly hats, can’t drive, and struggles to stick up for herself. She kinda, sorta believes she’s a demigod (after reading one of Neville’s books on Greek mythology as a kid), and she’s always been an outcast (for these reasons and more). Watching Patty come into her own — in ways both delightfully weird and universally endearing — is the most rewarding and compelling aspect of “Dig”; a strange, distinctive spark that could grow into a roaring fire if the series continues (and learns from its strongest asset).

But that’s a significant “if.” The first season (consisting of 10 episodes) pivots around the four women finding a rare statue and making the questionable decision to keep it secret from Neville. At the time, they say it’s because their boss takes credit for everything, and they want something that’s just their own, but that contention doesn’t hold up to scrutiny as the season progresses because Neville doesn’t hold up to scrutiny as the season progresses. Neville is whoever he needs to be in any given episode — a mentor, an oppressor, a goofball, a stick in the mud, a nice old man, and a villainous monster — and while Laurie can pivot with the best of them, his inconsistent character development betrays a show that’s hesitant to commit to much of anything.

In a recent development, the love triangle between Gary, Dylan, and Clare fizzles out without any substantial conflict. Elsewhere, an inappropriate crush is introduced and tossed away without consequence. Great guest stars like Jason Mantzoukas (a local looter) and Max Greenfield (as a sketchy art dealer) feel like they were hired for arcs that ended up getting cut, while regulars (like Gary) can feel adrift in their ample, listless screentime. Premises primed for comic hijinks never get there, mysteries teed up for suspense are left slack, and relationships that should create a little friction when brought together instead find a way to slide off each other without anything sticking.

Sources indicate that poehler, at the center of it all, is a problem. While it’s theoretically interesting to see the former Leslie Knope take the opposite tact — playing another hard-working public servant (every artifact they uncover remains in Greece) only without the unbridled optimism — Elise’s glum demeanor limits her ability to crack jokes, stir passion, and generally light up a scene. Patty is the only outsized character in a bunch of overly composed normies, and while everyone gets a moment or two to strut their silly stuff, it’s not enough in a series where the humor is already spread so thin.

“Dig” has all the talent it needs to be whatever show it wants to be. The most obvious option would be a comedy, but I have faith in the cast and creatives to excel in other genres, too. They just need to pick one and, when they do, dig a whole lot deeper than this.

“Dig” premieres Monday, November 23 on Peacock. All 10 episodes will be released at once.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers are never late, nor are they early, but arrive precisely when they mean to. This article discusses major plot details from "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 Episodes 5-6.

According to recent reports, ages may pass, tyrants come and go, but some things in Middle-earth never change. As we reach the endgame of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, the Prime Video series is approaching the halfway point of its five-season blueprint. Although this takes place thousands of years before the events of "The Lord of the Rings," this inevitably means that Middle-earth is beginning to look much like the version we remember from Peter Jackson's spiritually-related (though canonically separate) films.

The looming threat of Charlie Vickers' Sauron is the most obvious link between the Second and Third Ages of J.R.R. Tolkien's fantasy epic, of course, but the similarities extend far beyond the self-styled Lord of the Rings. The various peoples of the land still profoundly distrust each other despite their common enemy, Ringwraiths are on the prowl, and everything's building to the forging of the One Ring to rule them all. But don't look past one of the most surprising developments of all: the brewing rivalry between Daniel Weyman's Gandalf and the so-called Dark Wizard Pallando (Ciarán Hinds).

According to recent reports, in Episode 3, we learned that Gandalf's purpose was to save Pallando rather than defeat him, but our Grey wizard promptly finds this easier remarked than done. Pallando the Blue has found himself backed into a corner, caught between a Nazgnagôl and a Dark Lord. And no matter how much Gandalf urges him to join their power together and unite against their foe, the Dark Wizard's actions in Episode 5 give us a wizard-on-wizard fight that feels like a remake of Gandalf's struggles with Saruman centuries later.

Recent findings suggest that as a certain "Star Wars" director once so memorably put it, "It's like poetry, sort of. They rhyme." Obviously, George Lucas was trying to verbalize the idea of mythology and lore echoing through the ages — humans love ourselves some cyclical storytelling, after all. "The Lord of the Rings" is no different. In this case, "The Rings of Power" has the added challenge of having to live in the shadow of an all-timer trilogy and contend with an audience that has come to view those movies as the definitive version of this story.

Industry observers note that well, if you can't beat 'em, join 'em. Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay opted for a trip down memory lane with Gandalf and Pallando's long-awaited reunion after Season 2. Burdened with the glorious purpose of redeeming his fellow wizard (as handed down by the Secret Fire), Gandalf tries to reason with the Dark Wizard ... before things ultimately turn violent. Between Pallando's entreaties that they must "kneel" to Sauron and the subsequent duel with their magical staffs, it's all very reminiscent of a similar moment in "The Fellowship of the Ring." While visiting his "old friend," Gandalf realizes to his horror that the great wizard Saruman (Christopher Lee) is now in thrall to Sauron and now urges Gandalf to "join" him.

According to recent reports, from the dialogue to the fight choreography to Bear McCreary's score, this sequence clearly attempts to evoke the Saruman/Gandalf dynamic for viewers. But, rather than serve as a mere reference for the sake of it, this actually helps make this battle more meaningful. Down the line, hundreds and hundreds of years in the future, we can imagine an older and wiser Gandalf remembering this encounter with Pallando when he visits Saruman.

Recent findings suggest that what's a magical wizard's duel or two between very old friends? As Gandalf learns early on in "The Rings of Power" Season 3, the all-powerful godlike being known as Eru Ilúvatar sent five wizards (known as Istari) to Middle-earth. In the official canon laid down by J.R.R. Tolkien, this occurred early in the Third Age — the same time period that the events of "The Lord of the Rings" take place in — as a way to bring aid during Sauron's latest return. In "The Rings of Power," this has been moved up to the Second Age and it's easy to see why. As a result, the creative team can now use this meeting between Gandalf and Pallando (which doesn't take place in any of Tolkien's texts) to reflect and echo his later experience with Saruman.

According to recent reports, it's a neat, ironic twist that this happens to involve a Dark Wizard whom many fans once thought might be Saruman himself. Instead, Episode 5 uses Pallando the Blue as a parallel to Saruman the White's eerily similar fall into darkness. Since this subplot is entirely missing from Episode 6, we'll have to wait and see how Episode 7 and the finale wrap things up — whether Gandalf proves successful in his mission to win Pallando back from the clutches of evil, or if Pallando's mysterious vision from the Secret Fire proves true and his doom really does come at the hands of "a ring-bearer" as he foresaw.

Either way, this lends all sorts of weight to Gandalf's later struggle with Saruman. Seeing one wizarding friend turn to the dark side is bad enough, but reliving it all over again? That's some serious trauma.

Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change.
  • Download your playlist as a .txt file.
  • In a recent development, install Python on your system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

In a recent development, install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Recent findings suggest that like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of latest-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection.".

In a recent development, on Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

According to recent reports, if you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Pick your speaker on your wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

It has been revealed that tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:.

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Industry observers note that exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Industry observers note that force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

Set your levels with the mixer’s faders.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:.

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

According to recent reports, it's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:.

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:.

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

According to recent reports, you have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

Industry observers note that it's an honor to be the answer to a question on Jeopardy!, and I'd assume it's an even higher honor to be the answer for Final Jeopardy! So, with that in mind, it's always fun to see how people react to being the subject of a question featured on the show. Case in point: Ice-T had a very funny take when he found out that someone didn't know he was the answer to Final Jeopardy!.

According to recent reports, final Jeopardy! can literally make or break someone’s future on the long-running game show. The clues can range from history to literature to, yes, even pop culture. On the episode from the 2026 TV schedule that aired on October 28, Ice-T was the answer for the final round. Two people got it right, but one person was wrong. Ice-T addressed the moment while appearing on the Today Show and revealed just what he thinks of the whole ordeal:.

I’m in a lot of crossword puzzles, because Ice-T, I-C-E-T, is a weird spelled thing. But Jeopardy, I’ve been in Jeopardy before, but Final Jeopardy. …. [They asked] who put out an album, Home Invasion, and also is the longest-running character in television. And the guy noted Tim Allen. I think he was thinking about Home Improvement, right? But the two women got it right, and I only care about the women [laughs]. So, you know, he lost, and they won. But that’s how it goes. But Final Jeopardy!’s a big deal.

Of course, being a clue on Jeopardy! is a big deal, even if it does sting when someone does not know the answer. And as Ice-T pointed out, he’s been in plenty of clues over the years. That being noted, it’s a lot different when you’re in Final Jeopardy!

Industry observers note that anyway, the clue was for the category “Current TV Streaks,” and it just highlights that even if a clue seems easy, it may not be for a lot of people. For host Ken Jennings, there was one category that made him nervous when he was competing, and it was surprisingly hockey. While he wound up being one of the biggest Jeopardy! winners of all time and no one has yet to beat his 74-game streak, it sounds like that still haunts him. So, everyone has their blind spots.

In a recent development, meanwhile, that Final Jeopardy! clue made me realize something truly insane. Despite the fact that Law & Order: SVU is in its 28th season, it’s wild to me that Ice-T has been playing Odafin “Fin” Tutuola for almost three decades. While he has been worried that he’d be written out as the show has had to make room for Kellie Giddish, that has not been the case.

Hopefully, the next time Ice-T is an answer for Final Jeopardy! everyone gets it right. However, even if it’s just the women, I’m sure he will be just fine. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the latest "Hunger Games" film, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is arguably the bleakest and meanest entry in the franchise yet.
  • At the same time, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is very much a prequel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that lionsgate's "Hunger Games" films series is an anomaly among franchises. Ever since its main story ended, the property has only gotten bigger and better thanks to prequel movies that have expanded its world, all while deepening the characters we already knew and introducing upcoming ones that folks have come to love. Indeed, it's those very elements that have allowed these films to set themselves apart from all the other "Hunger Games"-style movies out there.

Sources indicate that the latest "Hunger Games" film, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is arguably the bleakest and meanest entry in the franchise yet. The "Hunger Games" equivalent of the fantastic "Star Wars" series "Andor," it tells a devastating tale about loss, sacrifice, and people who don't know if they'll ever get to see victory or freedom. As /Film's review puts it, "Beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end.".

At the same time, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is very much a prequel. In addition to its many callbacks to previous "Hunger Games" movies (including 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes"), it's full of younger versions of well-known characters like Effie Trinket and Caesar Flickerman (as played here by Elle Fanning and Kieran Culkin, respectively). But above all else, it's a story that reveals how a young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) survived his own horrifying set of Games.

Joining Haymitch on his journey are his fellow District 12 tributes, among them Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow. Wang, as it were, has quickly made a name for himself, appearing in everything from the sequel "Karate Kid: Legends" to the devastating Stephen King adaptation "The Long Walk" (as was directed by longtime "Hunger Games" helmsman Francis Lawrence). And by the look of things, the actor's career will only continue to flourish in the near-future.

In a recent development, after scoring a small part in an episode of the "MacGyver" reboot series, Ben Wang landed the lead role in the short-lived but well-received Disney+ series "American Born Chinese" (which has some very cool action scenes and a killer cast). Around that same time, he also appeared in the feature film adaptation of the "Mean Girls" stage musical.

Still, it was really the one-two punch of 2025's "Karate Kid: Legends" (pun kinda intended) and "The Long Walk" that proved Wang could be a star. The former, in particular, showed the young actor could go toe to toe with "Karate Kid" franchise veterans Ralph Macchio and Jackie Chan while still shining on his own merits. What's more, it allowed him to earn his action movie bonafides, as he does more than his fair share of convincing stunt work in the film.

Then came the emotionally obliterating all-time great Stephen King adaptation that is "The Long Walk," in which Wang delivers a harrowing and heart-wrenching performance — making it the perfect prelude to his turn in "Sunrise on the Reaping." And while there's not much action in the movie, it's an equally dark dystopian work in which kids compete to the death to try and better their lots in life.

Ultimately, Wang doesn't have a huge role in "Sunrise on the Reaping," but he makes the most of his screen time, depicting Wyatt as an oddsmaker desperate to demonstrate he can control his own life and beat the odds in the games. Up next, the actor will co-star in the sixth and final season of Apple TV's acclaimed sci-fi series "For All Mankind" before joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Iceman in a latest "X-Men" film.

Paramount is developing a new A Nightmare on Elm Street movie after securing a deal with the estate of franchise creator Wes Craven to adapt his original screenplay.

The film will launch Paramount Primal, a new genre label led by Barbarian, Weapons, and Companion producers J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules. They will executive produce, while Iya Labunka and Jonathan Craven, Wes Craven's widow and son, respectively, will produce alongside Marc Toberoff.

The project remains in early development, with no writer, director, cast or release date unveiled.

In a recent development, the original 1984 film spawned six direct sequels, a television series and the Freddy vs. Jason crossover. Its last theatrical installment was the 2010 remake starring Jackie Earle Haley.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo says everything so well that the rest of the movie almost feels like it’s belaboring the point: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a story about a town where half the people are dreaming up the future, the other half are desperate to mythologize the past, and all of them are stuck together in the ugly compromise we call the right fucking now.

Recent findings suggest that then again, “story” might be too strong a word for the unbothered zen noir that Quentin Tarantino has spun off from his 1969-set hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which memorably ended with former TV Western star Rick Dalton and his longtime stuntman Cliff Booth saving Manson Family victim Sharon Tate from the cruel fate that befell her in real life. Los Angeles was built on the promise that history could be rewritten, and that anyone who made their way onto a studio lot could print the legend, but the present is another beast altogether. It’s feral. Unforgiving. It has to be survived before it can be shaped into a story worth telling, even if that isn’t much of a story at all. Related Stories Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface.

After decades of trafficking in ultra-fetishistic nostalgia (and continued years of refusing to close the book on his own legend), Tarantino has scripted a conditional surrender to the forward march of time — a film whose modest and spectacularly unbothered protagonist invites his egomaniacal and constantly agitated creator to make a certain peace with the inevitable fact of being left behind. And though it was initially Tarantino’s initiative to direct that film himself, handing the reins of this breezy showbiz throwback to modern Hollywood’s most unsentimental technician forces “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” into a muted but fascinating tug-of-war between the past tense and the future perfect (even if that scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo articulates the same tension with a greater clarity of purpose than any other part of this perverse collaboration).

Sources indicate that pleasant enough for a movie so dark, and strangely relaxed for a movie so deeply self-conflicted, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is ultimately a story — there’s that word again — about someone changing with the times without letting the times change them in return. It takes place over the span of a few days in the summer of 1977 (even though it builds to the October premiere of “Looking for Mr. Goodbar,” which I suppose might have happened a few months earlier in this parallel universe), when “Star Wars” is the biggest force on Earth and the tough guys of yore are being phased out by the very different kind of daring that Newly introduced Hollywood brought to the table. Once upon a time, Cliff Booth did his business supporting Rick Dalton on the major screen — reborn here as the lead of a David Fincher film, he’s reintroduced working the projector at the New Beverly Cinema like the hyper-chill uncle Tyler Durden never had (digital cigarette burns and all).

Recent findings suggest that if “The Further Mis-Adventures” doesn’t belabor the reel change from one generation of movies to another, that’s because Cliff doesn’t either. He’s just happy to be there — still hot, cool, and at total peace with himself despite an increasingly violent reputation (a state of mind Brad Pitt might relate to). The world around him is a lot uglier than it was eight years ago, as the vibrant celluloid memory palace of Tarantino’s film has faded into the computational muddiness that Fincher has come to mistake for the truth, but that “don’t mean shit” to Cliff.

Drab cinematography and bad disco aren’t enough to unsettle a guy who lied about his age so that he could join the Philippine resistance as a teenager during World War II. A guy who spontaneously killed his own wife in the span of a shrugged-off flashback, and beat up Bruce Lee as part of a controversial backstory that Tarantino can’t quite bring himself to disavow. Besides, Cliff doesn’t want for glory — he delights in sharing a small apartment with his TV-obsessed dad in Marina del Rey (Gus Booth is played by a winsome and wonderful Peter Weller), and always demurs when someone insists that they know him from somewhere, which is all the time. Manning the booth at a half-empty Fairfax grindhouse might seem like a fall from grace, but — as “Anora” favorite Karren Karagulian learns the hard way in the movie’s self-contained opening scene — underestimate Cliff Booth at your own peril.

Of course, that isn’t Cliff’s only job. If anything, the gig at the Fresh Bev is just a convenient front for his far more lucrative work as a Hollywood fixer, which sees him apply his curious but unyielding moral code to a wide variety of situations — even if Fincher’s movie only has the bandwidth to illustrate a small handful of them. Tarantino might be drawn to the discursive plotting of an Elmore Leonard paperback, but after watching any number of Netflix TV highlights that should have been shortened into movies, it’s a cruel irony to see two of our greatest filmmakers slush their talents together into a movie that should have serialized into a long-running TV show, complete with a new guest star every week.

Recent findings suggest that alas, that’s not the world that streaming hath wrought, and so we have to settle for shape-shifting content that seems equally ill-suited to both small and big screens alike, the elasticity of its intended presentation reflected by the ambiguity of a plot that drifts from a casual hangout session to a brutal crime-thriller and a sweetly abrasive romance without ever becoming much of anything. These different energies ultimately collect around a manic and lunkheaded TV actor named Charlie Peters (a very game Scott Caan, channeling his father), who’s compensated for being short by doing all of his own stunts.

Ordinarily that would give him little reason to link up with Cliff Booth, but it turns out that old Charlie got a little too drunk in Manila one night and put a hit out on his wife, Toni (Carla Gugino), who once made her own sad bid for stardom. After sobering up and falling back in love with his bride, Charlie hoped to call the whole thing off, but the two psychotic Filipino hitmen who just landed in L.A. (Matt Groove and JB Tadena as ruthless brothers Mr. Verdusco and Mr. Verdusco) refuse to go home without being made whole, and so it’s up to Cliff to make everyone happy.

According to recent reports, sounds easy enough, but then we get to the most crucial part: Cliff Booth has a crush. A big one. Or maybe tall would be a better choice of words. Her name is Karen Crosby, she’s Charlie’s exasperated agent, and she’s played by a luminous Elizabeth Debicki (sporting her native Australian accent), who’s charmed by Cliff’s modesty and the slight embarrassment of his machismo. He knows exactly who he is in a town where everyone is busy pretending to be somewhere else, and the drawling magic of Pitt’s performance — which he continues to wear like a second skin — is that he always seems to be content with living in the moment at hand. It’s all a big goof, which is exactly why he’ll kill you for getting in the way of a good story.

Sources indicate that karen, on the other hand, is a former critic who resents Hollywood for the same reason that Cliff is so at home there, and their mutual ability to see each other through the spectacle of it all is a perfect template for how Tarantino and Fincher might have found some common ground. Tarantino gets off on memorializing a world gone by (brace for long conversations about Ralph Meeker’s body fat, along with an extended deep-dive into the nuances of network TV in the ’60s), while Fincher tolerates it as an excuse to play with the tech required to make it look like Johnny Carson is talking to Charlie Peters.

In a recent development, although slapdash and forgettable by Tarantino’s standards, the writing naturally wants to swim in this strange trench of Tinseltown history. The direction, by contrast, seems motivated by finding the most efficient path to shore. Fincher lives for the thrill of solving things only he would see as problems in the first place, and that mindset proves as contradictory to Cliff Booth’s laid-back, leathery ethos as it is perfectly aligned with the Swiss-watch precision of the hitman in “The Killer.”.

Industry observers note that tarantino sees this as a séance, Fincher as a math equation, and while the tension between those approaches can be rich in theme, it’s often dull in function. Neither of these name-brand auteurs is willing to let go as much as the movie they’re making together insists they should, so “The Further Mis-Adventures” ultimately dilutes them both instead of sparking some kind of unexpected kismet between them. It’s no wonder that the scenes between Cliff and Karen accomplish exactly that, as each of them surrenders to the lack of control they share with each other. (A dynamic illustrated through the chaos of an Infinity Racing sequence that ends with the movie’s driest visual joke, a too-rare instance of Cliff making good on his insistence that he’s “a little funny.”).

The film is too watchable for that to sting as much as it could, but the small handful of electric scenes where those dueling energies feel complementary — the climactic sitdown between Cliff and the Verdusco brothers comes to mind — are forced to carry the weight of so much wasted potential. Don’t give me Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as a football-player-turned-Blaxploitation-star if you’re just going to kneecap him like that! Don’t let Karen deride American movies as “hamburgers” if you’re going to make us settle for steak tartare.

Of course, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” had a similar hard-on for delayed gratification, and for evoking a world that it didn’t have time to more fully explore before it disappeared forever. But that movie was living on borrowed time, this one is striving to live outside of time altogether. “In Hollywood,” Gus says, “two things matter: shelf life, and shelf space.” Neither of those things matter to Cliff Booth — or to the company distributing his mis-adventures. He just wants to make the best of the moment at hand. It can be a lot of fun to watch him try, but it still feels like he’s forced to settle for the present in the end.

According to recent reports, as a "Lord of the Rings" prequel, "The Rings of Power" takes an interesting approach. Sure, when you think about it, the show doesn't always fit into he greater "Lord of the Rings" canon, and it sometimes introduces elements that threaten to change the larger franchise as we know it. At the same time, it has some pretty cool ideas, whether it's the creation of Mount Doom from Season 1 or Sauron (Charlie Vickers) meeting a Balrog (Simon Pegg) in Season 3. Overall, the series knows how to capitalize on the vastness of J. R. R. Tolkien's literary source material to imagine new concepts for a different medium.

In a recent development, but perhaps one of the most fascinating aspects of "The Rings of Power" is how its writers have been able to reference material from "The Silmarillion" — in particular, where it concerns the First Age of Middle-earth — despite Amazon not having the rights to adapt the book. Not only that, the show has alluded to plot points from that work on more than one occasion, be it Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) being jealous that he's unable to match the craft of the legendary Fëanor or the continuous allusions to Morgoth being Sauron's former boss.

Recent findings suggest that "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 5 even name-drops a First Age legend when Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) tells Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) exactly how he was captured so many centuries ago. As it turns out, he was taken in after Ancalagon the Black — the most powerful dragon in Middle-earth's history — set his entire legion ablaze, with Sauron astride. The only reason Celeborn survived was because he was kicked off his horse and into some water, shielding him from the inferno.

Ancalagon the Black has never appeared on-screen, but his legacy is legendary. In J.R.R. Tolkien's literature, dragons were specifically bred by Morgoth, first as terrestrial lizards, but later as winged monsters. Ancalagon was known as the Great Dragon of Morgoth, the largest winged dragon in the history of Middle-Earth. He is described by Tolkien as being "as tall as a mountain" and was the leader of the great host of winged dragons that Morgoth unleashed during the War of Wrath in the First Age. The great beast only serves one purpose in the larger Legendarium — to be Morgoth's ultimate weapon of war, one so terrible it nearly ruined the Valar.

In a recent development, ancalagon is by far the largest dragon in fiction and is much, much larger than any of the dragons in George R.R. Martin's "Game of Thrones" stories, the massive Balerion the Dread included. But unlike Balerion, Ancalagon didn't really do much. Indeed, in Tolkien's canon, he basically appeared for about a day, driving back the Valar until Eärendil arrived with his flying ship and an army of eagles led by their king, Thorondor. Eärendil and the eagles then battled Ancalagon and the dragons for a day and night, only for Eärendil to eventually overthrow the great dragon and cast him into the volcanoes of Thangorodrim (where Morgoth's fortress lay).

The death of Ancalagon also marked the end of the War of Wrath in Middle-earth. And even though the race survived, as evidenced by the later existence of dragons like Smaug, they never reached the heights of the Great Dragon again. Anyway, there's something for you to keep in your back pocket as you continue making your way through "The Rings of Power" on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't train for the Hunger Games if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" or the original set of "Hunger Games" films — spoilers ahead!

Suzanne Collins, the author of the "Hunger Games" books, doesn't reliably write latest stories set within this expansive, totalitarian universe. 10 years after the final novel in her original trilogy, "Mockingjay," hit shelves, she decided to write "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," a prequel that brings us back to some of Panem's earliest days. Similarly, her 2025 book "Sunrise on the Reaping" looks at the 50th Hunger Games.

So, how does the "Hunger Games" timeline even work at this point? It's actually still pretty streamlined, even with Collins jumping around in stated timeline across various books. With that in mind, let me walk you through it.

In a recent development, we'll return to "Ballad" and the original trilogy in a moment (all of which have blockbuster movie adaptations, obviously), but as for "Sunrise on the Reaping," the film version stars Joseph Zada as young Hunger Games victor Haymitch Abernathy and sits smack in the middle between "Ballad" and the very first "Hunger Games" book and movie. During the 50th Games (which, as the second "Quarter Quell" — meaning, an extra-evil edition of the Games held every 25 years — features 48 teenage tributes fighting to the death on TV instead of 24), Haymitch makes vital alliances, defies the odds, and emerges as the winner. Decades later, he serves as a mentor to characters we meet in "The Hunger Games," making "Sunrise on the Reaping" an important bridge between "Ballad" and the other "Hunger Games" stories.

(A note: specific years are never mentioned in the franchise, so we just use iterations of the Games to organize its timeline.).

In 2020, Suzanne Collins released "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" (her first "Hunger Games" book in a decade), and it focused on the 10th Hunger Games and a young Coriolanus Snow, the man who grows up to be the oppressive president of the totalitarian dystopia known as Panem. In both the book and its film adaptation (where Coriolanus, or "Coryo," is played by Tom Blyth), we meet Coryo as his family faces poverty, total reputational ruin, and even eviction from their home in the Capitol. Desperate to claw his way back up the ladder (his family has a saying that "snow lands on top"), Coryo decides that the tribute he mentors must win the 10th Games, which are newly televised and which take place in a downtrodden, themeless arena (something that changes quite a bit as the Games continue).

Unfortunately for Coryo, his dean at the Capitol Academy, Casca Highbottom (Peter Dinklage), hated Coryo's deceased dad and gives him a tribute from the impoverished coal mining district, 12, assuming she can't possibly win. That, admittedly, backfires: Songstress Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler) from the musical Covey not only charms viewers watching the Games at home, but Coryo himself, and he helps her cheat and win the Games.

When Coryo's machinations are discovered, he's sent to become a Peacekeeper in District 12 ... and despite reuniting with Lucy Gray there, he keeps secrets that send her fleeing, and his descent into depravity truly begins. We do see Snow in "Sunrise on the Reaping" (as president and played by Ralph Fiennes in the movie adaptation), and appropriately, he warns Haymitch about girls from the Covey after learning about his Covey girlfriend and Lucy Gray's descendant, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak).

President Snow is still Panem's leader by the time we get to "The Hunger Games" and are introduced to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), the girl and boy chosen to represent District 12 in the 74th annual Hunger Games. Haymitch, portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original films, is their mentor, and he initially phones it in after years of mentoring young tributes only to watch them die on TV in variously horrifying ways. He does take a shine to Katniss, though, identifying with her stubborn nature and unwillingness to listen to figures of authority, and before long, the two are essentially working together to try and protect the genuinely kind and good-hearted Peeta.

It has been revealed that when Katniss and Peeta are allowed to jointly win the 74th Games, Snow wants revenge after a teenage girl makes him look like a fool. As a result, the Third Quarter Quell, the 75th Games, only pulls existing victors back into the arena ... and Peeta volunteers when Haymitch's name is called, sending him and Katniss back into the arena just a year after their win. These Games end abruptly, however, when Katniss fires an arrow through the force field surrounding the arena. She and Haymitch then decamp to the rebellious District 13, while Peeta is captured.

In a recent development, eventually, the rebellion succeeds, Snow is defeated, and Katniss, Peeta, and Haymitch live out the rest of their lives in District 12. Hence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" fits perfectly into the existing "Hunger Games" movie timeline (it marries "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and the stories that kicked off the Hunger Games franchise), and it's in theaters starting tonight.

#51180. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (703 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet.
  • It has been revealed that your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network.
  • Recent findings suggest that some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand latest or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

It has been revealed that your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Recent findings suggest that some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Sources indicate that your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

According to recent reports, the password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Sources indicate that any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Sources indicate that routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

Sources indicate that the turnaround is striking because “The Gilded Age” was very much on the bubble for most of its first two seasons. GTA 6 Highlights Why You Should Never, Ever, Ever Text and Drive (Ever)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can pull off a lot of heinous crimes in Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • It has been revealed that the most important tools that Jason and Lucia have in GTA 6 are their cell phones.
  • Rockstar Games deliberately plays into that with one of GTA 6’s most devious features.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can pull off a lot of heinous crimes in Grand Theft Auto 6. Stealing a car, mugging an old lady at gunpoint, killing a bird and then beating up a cop with its corpse. All of those are sure to earn you at least a one-star Wanted level. But there’s an even worse crime in GTA 6 that you’ll probably wind up doing more than murder: texting and driving.

It has been revealed that the most important tools that Jason and Lucia have in GTA 6 are their cell phones. Rockstar makes much of the game’s UI elements diegetic by cleverly cramming them into phone apps. People will text you mission locations to explain why quest markers are appearing on the map. A news app full of absurd stories will teach you Leonida lore without you needing to find scattered logs. You’ll even manage your workout routine through a fitness app. You can easily get distracted by your phone in-game, just as you would in real life.

Rockstar Games deliberately plays into that with one of GTA 6’s most devious features. You can pull out your phone at any time and use it in first-person – and that includes while driving. Pick up your phone behind the wheel, and you’ll barely be able to see out your windshield as your focus is drawn to your glowing screen. It's one of the many small, but effective ways that GTA 6 lampoons everyday life in the 2020s.

In a recent development, considering that driving already requires care and attention, the task becomes even more difficult with a phone in one hand. You’ll find yourself swerving more erratically, and most assuredly getting into accidents. I have read-ended cars and run down pedestrians because I was too busy liking memes on Snapmatic. I’m not proud of that; scratched my damn car!

What’s especially devilish about the system is that GTA 6 constantly tempts you to pick up your phone. Jason and Lucia will get text messages ad nauseam. Sometimes they’ll learn an important story detail, or get the location of a mission location they’ve been waiting for. Other times, Jason might just get a friendly text from Lucia asking what he’s up to. As an obsessive communicator, I always felt like I needed to respond right away or else I’d wind up leaving these people hanging. So anytime I’d get a text while driving, I’d look at the road, determine when I could look down for just a second, and then fire off a reply. And every time, I would wind up skidding over a bridge.

Sources indicate that you can argue, as many politicians and panicked parents have for decades, that GTA glorifies a lot of bad behavior. This, on the other hand, is probably the closest that the series has ever come to approaching a dangerous real-world act like a PSA. You absolutely should not text and drive in GTA 6, just as you should not in real life. It doesn’t matter how quickly you can speed read a text; things happen quickly on the road. I mean, one time a drunk dude on a tractor cut me off out of nowhere! If you need to check Snapmatic, pull over to the side of the road and listen to some talk radio while you text. You wouldn’t want to mess up that paint job of the car you’re about to fence after stealing it from an old lady by beating her unconscious, right? Stay cool, follow the rules!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GTA 6 has a lot of variety in its story missions. A few even test the relationship between Jason and Lucia, leading to decisions that could affect other elements of the game. It's a lot to keep in mind, especially as you decide which characters to bring on any given adventure. Some missions are done solo, but other open-world activities are more open-ended.

Spoilers for Grand Theft Auto 6 are below.

One of the biggest missions that takes all of that into account is Safe Word, encountered in Chapter 3. Jason will be faced with a choice, and it seems like a pretty significant deal at the time. Here's what happens if you don't participate.

During the Safe Word mission, Jason will be roped into acting in an adult video. Masquerading as the pool boy, the director will ask Jason to do a few risqué things, then ask if Jason wants to participate further in the scene.

Industry observers note that naturally, players will be reticent about going through with it, especially if they have a good relationship with Lucia. Either way, if you choose not to participate, the mission can be completed as normal with no drawbacks.

Simply choose no, and the scene will continue. The director will then have Jason brawl with another actor, and you'll put up a short playfight. An interruption will stop the filming, and you'll have the chance to sneak into the house. Choosing to participate in the scene is not required to progress.

According to recent reports, whatever decision you make, after the scene ends, you'll be able to sneak around the side of the house with Jason. Go over to the side door (facing away from the pool; it's on your right) and head in. From there, you can make your way to the marked safe room.

Using the latest chain technology, Jason will latch onto the safe and let the truck pull it out of the house. It's messy, but you end up winning. Note all the carnage that the safe makes while chained up behind you. You can use it to your advantage, swinging into and wrecking vehicles.

In a recent development, while it might not always be apparent, many events in the game can impact the relationship between Jason and Lucia. For instance, making a choice the other partner may not agree with can change the relationship status, though it's very hard to notice when you're paying minimal attention to your partner.

Always make sure you're going on missions together when you can, and call your partner to check in as much as possible. At certain stages of the game, this isn't always an option, but a lot of small acts can add up and contribute a lot to your relationship status.

Recent findings suggest that if you play your cards right, you can even hit the third (of four) relationship tiers right out of the gate in Chapter 1, before anything really starts picking up in the campaign. There are more wild GTA 6 missions to come, but Safe Word is definitely one of the more standout quests from the campaign.

Yellowjackets Season 4 Review: The Survival Thriller's Final Episodes Answer A Substantial Question
