Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about.
  • Recent findings suggest that the documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing.
  • According to recent reports, now Latest York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about. First-time feature filmmaker Brydie O’Connor’s Sundance-winning documentary “Barbara Forever” is a hypnotic archival collage that retraces the life, work, and death of Barbara Hammer.

Recent findings suggest that the documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing. (Kristen Stewart also jumped on board as an executive producer.) It’s not hard to see why. “Barbara Forever” is an archival documentary that unfolds in the shape and style of its subject, an experimental filmmaker who put together some of the first publicly projected lesbian erotica actually made by a lesbian. Voiceover by the filmmaker spans her early career in the Bay Area (and halcyon days as an out lesbian), her 1992 feature debut “Nitrate Kisses,” and the final years of a cancer battle that ended in 2019. Related Stories Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break.

According to recent reports, now Latest York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met. “I read about Barbara and studied Barbara before I even saw her films,” O’Connor told IndieWire. She reached out to Hammer to “buy her DVDs because they weren’t showing anywhere in D.C. And she wrote back to me. At first, she was a little bit hard on me. She was like, ‘I see you’re writing from an edu.edu address. I just want to make sure that you’re actually a student because if you’re faculty, it would be much, much more expensive.’ [Laughs] And I stated, ‘I promise, Barbara, I’m a student. I just can’t wait to see your movies.’ And she sent me her DVDs. So yeah, I think that initial impulse to explore her work was really about … ‘Why don’t more people know about Barbara and her work?'”.

Hammer had degrees in psychology and literature before encountering “Meshes of the Afternoon” director Maya Deren’s films (which also influenced David Lynch) at San Francisco State in the 1970s. They lit the fuse for making her own movies. Circa that time, she’d been living in Santa Rosa and married to a man. She came out as a lesbian — busting through that closet, really, with abandon — and took off with her Super 8 camera to start making lesbian films. Growing up in Kansas, O’Connor, in her early 30s, resonated with Hammer’s early biography, and Hammer’s early lust for self-reinvention.

“She was not really tentative about anything. She picked up a camera in her late 20s as she was getting a divorce from a man when she realized that she was a lesbian and she made her film,” O’Connor said. “She learned by doing. And I was so inspired because, at the time, I was studying American studies and history in school. I had no background in the arts really, except for enjoying consuming them. And I really thought I would be a film critic or a writer… [Barbara Hammer] was not afraid to fail creatively. And she tried so many different ideas, of course, throughout her entire career in making over 85 films, but especially in that first decade of her career.”.

According to recent reports, post-college and in Upcoming York, O’Connor, who’s spent “a decade in the Hammer world, and my entire adult consciousness,” would see Hammer at the Metrograph in Lower Manhattan. “I definitely was ‘the girl who wrote her thesis on Barbara,’ probably one of many, and I was day-playing in the film industry,” O’Connor said. “I would occasionally go up to Yale, where her formal archive is held, to continue doing independent research. I was looking at her love letters and her photographs… I wrote to her in January of 2019 when I was about to make my first short film. I said, ‘Hi, Barbara.’ I didn’t know how sick she was at the time. I was like, ‘I’m making my first film. Can I take you to coffee? Do you have any advice for me?’ And she wrote back to me and said, ‘I’m at the very, very end of my life, but best of luck with everything in your career.'”.

Hammer died in March 2019, which is when O’Connor contacted the filmmaker’s partner, the human rights advocate Florrie Burke. “Florrie was the love of her life. They were together for 31 years,” O’Connor said. Their meeting culminated in O’Connor’s 2022 short film “Love, Barbara,” which she expanded into the feature that hit theaters this year. In a 2026 Oscar documentary race heavy on genocide and social complications — or a three-hour A24 movie that’s shaken up the entire form — “Barbara Forever” is life-affirming, lovely, yet still-important counter-programming.

It has been revealed that the organic archival rhythm of “Barbara Forever” eschews talking heads altogether, instead conversing with what Hammer’s work looked and felt like. One of the film’s most charming snippets finds Hammer showing one of her (SFW!) films to a classroom of small schoolchildren. They end up having an unexpected appreciation for the experimental film clip’s non-narrative sensibilities.

Industry observers note that O’Connor collaborated with Burke on sifting through 35 hours of audio recordings to stitch together a narration unfolding entirely in Hammer’s own words. “Florrie was so happy with [the short], but she always reminded me there’s so much more to Barbara than just our relationship,” O’Connor mentioned. “Barbara’s this huge personality. She’s so charismatic and charming and really both thoughtful, but also very savvy. She wanted to be recognized. She wanted to be known for her work and her efforts, and she was uncompromising in what she made and how she shared her work. So it just made sense that she would be the narrator of the film.”.

The Sundance-winning editing, too, proved a challenge, as O’Connor and her filmmaking team pored over more than 400 hours of visual material — from Hammer’s films, to outtakes, B-sides, home videos, and more. “I really wanted to convey with this film: Why did Barbara turn the camera on herself and her life and her lovers and her body as a method of alternative history making? What did she see in the value of that approach and then making experimental cinema out of it and demanding the value of that within culture?”.

That Hammer’s work wasn’t more canonized during her life — an effort O’Connor has made partly her own, especially as a newly introduced digital restoration of “Nitrate Kisses” is making the rounds — isn’t only because of how confrontational she was about gender and her own sexuality. “Nitrate Kisses” is, after all, an experimental movie about lesbian repression dating back to the early 20th century. Is it also that autofiction and individualism, now a dominant mode of contemporary artistic expression, were also marginalized at that point within her particular corner of the art world?

In a recent development, “She was both an experimental filmmaker and avant-garde artist and a lesbian filmmaker. And she says, and this was something she stated all throughout her life and career, that she didn’t fit neatly into either category where she could just build an audience within that space,” O’Connor said. “She really was uncompromising about being both and working at the intersection of both and having both audiences… The experimental film world didn’t necessarily want to see lesbian work, didn’t necessarily want to see the nude woman’s body on screen. And lesbians, there was not so much representation, especially in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, increasingly so, but her work was experimental and thought-provoking, and she felt like a lot of her queer audiences wanted more realistic depictions of queerness.”.

O’Connor, who received a 2026 Creative Capital to not only finish her work on “Barbara Forever” but also continue making docs, noted, “The industry is hard, but that certainly won’t stop me from making nonfiction films. I’m just excited to pivot to my next project.”.

“Barbara Forever” is now available to stream on PVOD platforms.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

According to recent reports, is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

According to recent reports, if your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it substantial and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

In a recent development, want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

Recent findings suggest that if you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous latest reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

It has been revealed that if you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend indicates a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

It has been revealed that the one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it indicates up in the Find My app.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Recent findings suggest that MOFT has been making the origami-style folding wallet for many years, and this model works like any other Find My accessory. So that means you get left-behind alerts when you leave without it, and the ability to make it trackable through Apple’s network if it’s across town instead of under the couch. It also works with Google’s Find Hub on Android, which matters if you’ve got a mixed household of devices.

Recent findings suggest that the wallet is powered by a built-in battery rather than a watch-style battery, and MOFT says a charge lasts about six months. You charge it by placing the wallet on a Qi charger for about an hour and a half, which, in practice, means dropping it on a MagSafe dock twice a year. That’s a better setup than an AirTag in a wallet as well.

Recent findings suggest that the wallet holds up to eight cards, or closer to four to six if you also use the hidden compartment for cash. A pull tab in the wallet brings your everyday cards out in one motion, while your driver’s license and cash stay tucked inside of it. It’s made from MOFT’s vegan leather and at 14 mm thick, it’s slimmer than a traditional wallet but noticeably thicker than Apple’s card-only wallet, which is the price you are going to pay to hold up this much stuff.

Recent findings suggest that the stand is the usual MOFT origami fold-out, and it works in portrait and landscape for FaceTime or watching a video on the plane. You can buy it without the stand if you’d rather have the thinner version. It comes in Jet Black, Misty Cove, Terracotta, and Peony.

In a recent development, two things to know going in. There’s no RFID blocking in this version (MOFT has a non-Find My Snap Field Wallet if you want that). MOFT also warns that the magnets can affect magnetic-stripe cards, so avoid putting a hotel key in it.

It has been revealed that I’ve spent the past month on a Pelican accessory beat, using wallets designed for outdoor use. #51155. The 10 Best Songs on the 'GTA 6' Soundtrack, Ranked

The 10 Best Songs on the 'GTA 6' Soundtrack, Ranked

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, to say there’s been a lot of hype and anticipation around Grand Theft Auto VI is like the understatement to end all understatements.
  • Recent findings suggest that they’ve been giant steps forward technologically while also dealing with some more dramatic things narratively.
  • According to recent reports, on the nose, sure, but if you’ve played a GTA game, you're surely aware that it’s not always the most subtle series in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, to say there’s been a lot of hype and anticipation around Grand Theft Auto VI is like the understatement to end all understatements. Grand Theft Auto V came out more than 13 years ago, and it was pretty mind-blowing at the time, as was Grand Theft Auto IV about five and a half years before that. The series has always been praised for the freedom it gives you, and lots of that freedom has also made the series controversial, but the last three games have done a whole lot more than just feel like mindless fun.

Recent findings suggest that they’ve been giant steps forward technologically while also dealing with some more dramatic things narratively. You get the best of all the worlds, because much of the gameplay is still heightened and you can keep on causing mayhem if you want to. Anyway, that’s skipping over a lot, and it’s not even touching on the music, but music has always been a substantial part of these games, even going back to the GTA games of the PS2/original Xbox era. And GTA 6 is no exception, having an impressive official soundtrack (34 original songs made for the game itself), and a score by Justice… and then, of course, all the licensed music. There is so much licensed music heard on the radio stations in this game, so highlighting some of the best songs from that huge soundtrack is only scratching the surface, but these are indeed some of the greatest tracks you can listen to – mostly when you're in a (probably stolen) car – while playing GTA 6.

According to recent reports, on the nose, sure, but if you’ve played a GTA game, you're surely aware that it’s not always the most subtle series in the world. That’s especially so for the satire, and while this writer hasn’t played enough of the most recent game to compare the humor to the previous games, many of those previous games took a South Park approach to comedy, satirizing/parodying pretty much everything that could be a decent target.

It has been revealed that so, it’s on-the-nose. And speaking of, there’s a song on the GTA 6 V-Rock FM station called “Lawyers, Guns, and Money,” and at least two of those things are very relevant to a game where you're stealing stuff and doing acts of violence. It’s a great song on its own (Warren Zevon has a deserved cult following, but probably deserves even more popularity), and it fits the mood of driving around GTA 6 remarkably well.

Industry observers note that this one is also a bit on-the-nose, or maybe obvious, and then further, it is a somewhat cheesy song. But… GTA 6 is a love story, given you can switch between playing two characters who are in a relationship (one with its ups and downs, sure, but that relationship is a central point of the whole game). They're Jason and Lucia, rather than Jack and Diane, but “Jack & Diane” is a broad, sweeping sort of song that really works with GTA 6’s main characters and then also, a little more abstractly, the setting/style.

The game probably elevates the song here, since in some contexts, this John Mellencamp track can feel like it lays it on a bit thick in a bad way. Maybe you just have to be in a certain mood to really appreciate it or vibe with it, but the mood can quite easily be felt while playing GTA 6, and hey, if a game or movie makes a song better, and the song sounds great as part of the soundtrack, why not include it for a ranking like this one?

If not “Pink Pony Club,” then Chappell Roan’s signature song to date is probably “Hot to Go!”, even if it might not even be her best song. It’s a substantial one, though. And it is fun. It’s a good fit for Flash FM, which is the modern (or fairly modern, maybe like 21st-century) pop radio station for GTA 6. Something a little moodier like “Good Luck, Babe!” might not have fit the vibe quite as well.

It’s pretty wild how good The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess is, as an album, that “Hot to Go!” is surrounded by a handful of songs that are even hotter. Also, seeing songs this recent is pretty great, just for the GTA 6 soundtrack generally, since the game was in development so long that there might've been something of a fear of things (music included) feeling dated by the time the game eventually came out.

In a recent development, it’s risky taking a song that was made for another property and putting it in something newly introduced, but it can be done, as “If You Leave” and its inclusion in GTA 6 shows. Like, this one isn't just associated with the 1986 movie Pretty in Pink because that movie happened to use the song well, but the song itself was made for that movie’s soundtrack, not appearing on an Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark studio album first.

Confusingly, the song “Pretty in Pink” was not written for the movie, but the movie was named after that Psychedelic Furs song. Also, that movie’s soundtrack is much better than the movie (it also features tracks by the likes of New Order, Echo & the Bunnymen, and The Smiths). That’s thankfully not the case with GTA 6. It’s a great game that just so happens to also have a great soundtrack, thanks to songs like “If You Leave.”.

Sources indicate that now for something a bit more recent, “Lost…” well, actually, it’s not so recent that it couldn’t have technically snuck onto the GTA 5 soundtrack. It’s one of the highlights off Frank Ocean’s 2012 album Channel Orange, and GTA 5 came out in 2013, so it could've potentially just snuck on. It’s also one of those cases where it might not be the artist’s very best song, but it’s up there, and it’s also one of the most appropriate for inclusion on a GTA soundtrack.

It has been revealed that it would be awesome to blast “Pyramids,” sure, but that song’s 10 minutes long, and you're not often going to be in a car for that long, since you'll probably get distracted by something on foot or hijack another vehicle or something in that time. And there are plenty of great songs from Blonde, but that’s more of a full album-listening experience, meaning songs plucked from there and put onto a more fractured soundtrack might not hit quite the same.

This one feels a little special, since you do hear “Drive” very early on as a needle drop, like right when you're supposed to drive to a location. Again, it’s a bit on-the-nose, but it does feel like a spontaneous and cinematic moment. The drive that you do when “Drive” is playing isn't even that wild or anything, but it’s the first time you'll be driving at night, and it is quite a quietly powerful experience.

Industry observers note that it’s the right song for that mood, and that makes it stand out a bit more, but hey, a soundtrack choice is a soundtrack choice. Oh, and the band is called The Cars, in case a song called “Drive” being in a game called “Grand Theft Auto 6” wasn’t already beating you over the head too much. Still, a great moment is a great moment, and this song is also just a flat-out great one, so all’s fair here.

According to recent reports, yes, yes, lots of pop and alternative/rock kinds of songs here, and those are the songs that sound best with the style and world of GTA 6, but there is a wider variety of music found here, as is the case with all the GTA games and their radio stations. The Chamber 106.6 has some heavier stuff, like metal and a bit of punk, with Metallica (admittedly about as popular as metal bands get) being well-represented.

There are three Metallica songs that can be heard on The Chamber 106.6, and “Master of Puppets” is probably the most exciting one to hear when you're driving at a very high speed, and especially so if you're driving fast and away from a bunch of cops. It makes an already vibrant and energetic game feel more so, and it’s also a hard-to-fault song in general, so it’s a great fit for GTA 6, obviously.

It’s weird to think about “Electric Feel” feeling nostalgic, since it came out around the same time as Grand Theft Auto 4, and that game is only two GTAs ago. Maybe time flies. Anyway, “Electric Feel” was popular, sure, but it also felt like it was just cool enough to be alternative, but then it was also punchy enough to not feel out of place on mainstream radio, so if you liked any kind of music about 18 or 19 years ago, there’s a good chance you dug this one.

In a recent development, as for other MGMT songs? Yeah, they're a good band, or duo, technically. There’s some good stuff beyond just the songs that became surprising hits.

And it has that synthy feel that makes it feel appropriate with GTA 6 and its Vice City (and beyond) setting. Sure, not as 1980s and synthy in the way that the ‘80s-set GTA: Vice City was, way back when that came out, but the whole location has clearly retained aspects of that era. As for other MGMT songs? Yeah, they're a good band, or duo, technically. There’s some good stuff beyond just the songs that became surprising hits, especially with the slightly more recent – and overall underrated – album Little Dark Age.

“This Is the Day” best and most succinctly lays out the appeal of the artist behind it. Remarked artist is The The, which has always been a headache of a band name, though it’s one of those bands that’s really just one guy (named Matt Johnson). Everyone else comes and goes, a bit like a karma chameleon or something. Anyway, The The isn't a household name, but “This Is the Day” is fairly well-known, partly because it was heard on the Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 soundtrack, and now it’s made its way into GTA 6 as well.

It’s one of a handful of lengthy and emotionally complicated songs found on the pretty much perfect album Soul Mining, with this track in particular striking such an admirably unique tone. It sounds a bit different depending on how you're feeling when you hear it, which is always a great quality for a song to have. If you hear it on Vice City FM (which is probably the best radio station in the game) while driving when the sun’s coming up in game, it always feels great, not to mention truly cinematic.

“Just Like Heaven” comes from what might be The Cure’s most sprawling – and perhaps messiest – album, Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me. “Messy” isn't bad, though; it’s more just that it’s eclectic to the point of being a little inconsistent, which is something that’s harder to say about some of the band’s other albums from the 1980s. But “Just Like Heaven” is a highlight, and so it making the cut for the GTA 6 soundtrack is cool (if you could only pick one Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me track).

Recent findings suggest that that album definitely has value alone for housing this song. “Just Like Heaven” does sound like that, being a truly euphoric pop song, maybe a little alternative, but not as alternative as most songs by The Cure. They went broad here, and they did it well (the same can be said for songs that aren’t found on any GTA 6 radio station, like “Boys Don’t Cry,” “Lovesong,” and “In Between Days”).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this year’s TIFF and Venice were quieter in terms of breakout sales, especially when compared to last year’s splash for “Obsession,” and several awards contenders were scooped up before they even premiered at the festival. But other smaller buyers have emerged in recent weeks to release some of the more critically acclaimed titles that didn’t land major sales ahead of time.

The festivals are long done, but we’re still tracking every sale that happens, so check back frequently.

In a recent development, distributor: MagnoliaDirector: Kris ReyFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: Not unlike Jordan Firstman going from comedian to unexpected leading man and festival circuit darling, Caleb Hearon earned some praise for his leading man turn in “Trash Mountain,” a dark comedy he wrote and starred in along with Zooey Deschanel that grapples with grief and growing up. Kris Rey directed the film that premiered at TIFF and was produced by “Jurassic World” filmmaker Colin Trevorrow. The film also stars Jacki Weaver, Jaboukie Young-White, and Kyle Marvin and was co-written by Ruby Castor. Curiously, Lilly Wachowski was at one point attached to direct the film before Rey came aboard. Magnolia now is planning a theatrical release in 2027. Related Stories ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ Comes to VHS in Special Pan-and-Scan Edition from Mutant ‘Epic Zombie Christmas,’ Family Comedy About Senior Citizens and Teenagers Making a Horror Film, Begins Production.

Distributor: Kino LorberDirector: Maiken BairdFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: This documentary about Palestinian-American author and intellectual Edward Stated earned strong reaction in its premiere at TIFF and festivals like NYFF and IDFA, in part because though he’s been dead for over 20 years, his writing and his views have been far more relevant in a post-October 7 landscape. IndieWire’s review out of TIFF praised the construction of the documentary and how it manages to be decades-spanning and comprehensive in a manageable running time. And Anne Thompson spoke with the filmmakers about the challenges of making the documentary and the fear that it being about Palestine would pose barriers to a distributor stepping up to buy it. Thankfully, Kino Lorber did just that, and it will be planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Industry observers note that distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she intends an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

In a recent development, distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, Upcoming Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”.

According to recent reports, distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

In a recent development, distributor: Black BearDirector: Nahnatchka KhanFestival: TIFF MarketBuzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Distributor: 1-2 SpecialDirector: Jacqueline LentzouFestival: Venice OrizzontiBuzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Industry observers note that distributor: Sony PicturesDirector: Roshan SethiFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic MonsterDirector: Joshua GiulianoFestival: TIFF Midnight MadnessBuzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Tech giant and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

Distributor: HBO Documentary FilmsDirector: Rebecca HunttFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

In a recent development, distributor: Roadside Attractions and VerticalDirector: Lauren Miller RogenFestival: TIFF Gala PresentationBuzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

It has been revealed that “Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

Distributor: Focus FeaturesDirector: Simon StoneFestival: Telluride and TIFFBuzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

According to recent reports, distributor: NetflixDirector: Danny BoyleFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.
